Zondo Commission Wrap end 2019

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We take a look back at the first 16 months of the Zondo Commission

Unique Selling Point:
The Zondo Commission into State Capture is one of the most important commissions in the history of South Africa's democracy but 16 months since it first started sitting, how effective has it been?

Summary:
Since it first started sitting in August 2018, there have been so many huge headlines to come out of the Zondo Commission that have shown the extent of State Capture. But this daily drip-drip of news has almost in a way desensitised the average South African citizen from the shocking stories that have come out of the commission.

16 months since it's inception, it's time to take a look back at what has been accomplished thus far.

What has been the most important information to have emerged from witness testimony. Who have been the most important people to have made submissions at the commission, from the whistleblowers to the people who’ve been accused in engaging in State Capture.

How long before the commission ends and what will be done with the evidence gathered?

For the piece we will interview the people such as Thuli Madonsela, journalists who’ve been covering the story, as well as a spokesmen from organisations like Corruption Watch. Finally we will also obtain objective and legal analysis from constitutional law professor Pierre De Vos.

We will provide insight into the effectiveness of the commission’s work to date. How long is the commission expected to sit for and when can we expect a final report? Are Commissions of Inquiry effective in South Africa or do they merely whitewash (Seriti & Farlam Commission for example), What will be done with the evidence gathered by the Commission? Will anyone be charged and prosecuted?

Expert:
Ms. Thuli Madonsela
Mr. Pierre De Vos
Miss. Sarah Smit M&G Jounalist
Miss. Valencia Talane Senior Journalist - Corruption Watch
Mr. Raymond Zondo DCJ Leader of the Zondo Commission

Press Release:


The Chronicle of Capture Unravelled
It’s been 16 months of gruelling testimony over detailed allegations of State capture. The mechanics of corruption have been laid bare. There’s been jostling over who would be called to account. Sitting down with – among others – Prof. Thuli Madonsela whose work paved the way for the Zondo Commission of Inquiry, Carte Blanche analyses the meaning of the painful revelations before the commission, over some of the country’s most shameful lapses in governance. We ask what has really been accomplished to date, and how the assembled evidence will feed into prosecutions to redeem a nation’s future.
Producer: Julian Sun
Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


V/O: State Capture

An insidious form of corruption

That wormed its way into the very heart of South Africa’s democracy

Tainting politicians

Plundering state resources

Hollowing out the very institutions meant to prevent it

How did it come to this?

LINK 1: The Zondo Commission of Inquiry into State Capture is without doubt the biggest political show in town. For the past 16 months it’s been shining a daily light on the shocking level of corruption that has by some reports cost South Africa R1,5 trillion.

V/O: Since August 2018, South Africans have sat riveted to their screens as a commission of inquiry, chaired by Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo, goes about the mammoth task of investigating state capture.

Faced with so many jaw dropping headlines, it’s easy to lose sight of how it came about in the first place.

Constitutional Law Professor Pierre De Vos explains.

Pierre De Vos Comment

LINK TO THULI: Since it began it has focused on alleged corruption identified in former public protector Thuli Madonsela’s State of Capture Report, in particular the infamous Gupta family, their access to State Owned Enterprises and their undue influence on the Zuma Administration.

THULI: What has happened is far more than I thought. A theatre of surprises and extremes

Her report envisaged a commission of inquiry that would sit for 180 days, yet the Zondo Commission is in 17th month of testimony. So is the former public protector surprised by how long the process is taking?

THULI: It has taken so long if it was investigated according to my methodology, the expanded terms means it has had to go beyond the original scope.

V/O: Deputy Chief Justice Raymond Zondo knows that the eyes of the country are upon him and the responsibility he carries in leading the commission.

A huge responsibility, a team of dedicated professionals that ensure that the work of the commission is done. It is very important for the country. If it’s successful, it can make a big contribution to SA

V/O: The Zondo Commission has been one of the biggest events of 2019, regularly making front-page news.

It began in January when Angelo Agrizzi revealed that Bosassa spent between R4 and R6-million monthly for bribes to senior government officials on the company’s payroll.

His explosive testimony shocked journalists covering the proceedings

Intro Valencia & Sarah, include a sound up from Agrizzi interview

Bossasa Beat

V/O: In October the former President’s son Duduzane Zuma initially testified that Thuli Madonslea did not give him a chance to comment before she released her report.

V/O: As a result he admitted that he did in fact get an invite to attend a meeting with the public protector


V/O: The Commission relies heavily on accounts given by whistle-blowers, several of whom have paid a heavy price for speaking up, such as former Trillian CEO Bianca Goodson

Whistleblowers: Jonas, Maseko, Mentor

the courage of some of the individuals who’ve come forward to give evidence, against all kinds of challenges because they believe the nation needs to know what they know. I have no doubt that some of them have done so in circumstances that their own friends wouldn’t want them to do it but they’ve done it because of their devotion to their country


V/O: But without doubt the most anticipated appearance at the commission came in July, when former President Jacob Zuma took the stand. Many hoped he’d use the opportunity to tell his side of the story but were left disappointed when he threatened to walk out of the commission and accused it of unfair cross-examination.

V/O: And just last week, former spy boss Mo Shaik told the commission that President Zuma stopped a wide-ranging investigation into the Gupta’s business empire and their influence on him.

V/O: What has been most shocking is that the evidence to date has revealed the depth of State Capture and how hollowed-out state institutions have become

There’s no doubt, there are things that have shocked me tremendously. If that is really true, what does this really mean in terms of what people are capable of doing. What does it mean for the country? If some of these things happened because some people didn’t do their job, then we need to deal with that in the report.


V/O: But is there a danger that daily revelations from the commission are desensitizing an already cynical-public to the level of corruption that has occurred?

Comments from journalist


I’m very hopeful and confident that arrests will happen, prosecutions will happen and a number of convictions.


The terms of reference tell us that, but as things stand, we are looking to try and finish the work next year. Our target is to try and finish oral evidence by midyear 2020. Whatever happens we want to submit the report to the president by the end of the year.
V/O: To date the Zondo Commission has already cost the tax payer R356 million. Has it been money well spent?



This is VIP because the main part of the investigations relates to people who weren’t voted in by the people of South Africa are alleged to have taken over the running of the country. This goes to the core of our democracy. Every 5 years we vote to put people into positions to run the country. Voters will feel deeply offended that people who weren’t voted in run the country. The allegations are being looked at by the commission. Who were the participants, who benefited, did people do their job? Were they willing participants? The country need to know this

My message is 2 fold – to thank SA from all walks of life for the support they have given. 2 I continue to urge those who have evidence to come forward. So that we have a good chance to understand what actually happened
